Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) sell to many of the same corporate customers, and both are betting that AI agents, software that can carry out tasks on its own, will become a major source of revenue.

Today, Microsoft got an uncomfortable reminder of how much those customers rely on it. A global outage that started Thursday afternoon knocked Outlook and parts of Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services offline for millions of users, and it dragged into Friday after the first fixes didn't hold. Microsoft says it has found no sign of malicious activity.

Microsoft shares are down around 1.5% in premarket trading on Friday. Salesforce has had a tough year of its own, with the stock down about 18% year to date.

RBC analyst Rishi Jaluria covers both tech giants and published notes on each this week, ahead of Microsoft's Ignite conference (November 17-20) and Salesforce's fiscal third-quarter report on December 2.

Microsoft

Starting with Microsoft, the analyst expects Ignite to show how far the company has pushed AI into every layer of its business, from data centers and in-house chips to apps and security. However, he doesn't see the event moving the stock much in the short term.

The backdrop is strong. Azure grew 48% in constant currency last quarter, up from 43% the quarter before, and management has guided for 49% to 50% this quarter. Jaluria believes demand still outruns the capacity Microsoft can bring online, which makes that guidance look cautious, though the year-ago comparison is a tough one. He wants updates on capacity and on Maia 300, the custom chip unveiled in October, which Microsoft is designing to be 40% more efficient than leading GPU setups and expects to roll out at multi-gigawatt scale in 2027.

Then there's Copilot. Daily users jumped about 50% from the prior quarter and more than fivefold year over year, while customers with over 50,000 Microsoft 365 seats grew more than 8x. Jaluria thinks investors are overlooking Microsoft's shift toward usage-based pricing, which Cowork and GitHub Copilot already use. Charging for consumption rather than per user could lift the ceiling on what Microsoft earns as agents take on more work, and he expects Ignite to add new agent-building and management tools.

Key Points

Revenue and earnings declined year over year: Q2 revenue fell 16.8% to CAD 103.4 million, while adjusted EBITDA dropped to CAD 8.3 million. Cost cuts helped margins improve sequentially to 8%, up from 5.2% in Q1.

Bookings exceeded revenue: Quarterly bookings rose 22% from Q1 to CAD 108.2 million, for a 1.05 book-to-bill ratio. Alithya is shifting toward higher-margin work, including fixed-price projects, while Salesforce delays and Quebec restructuring weigh on results.

Alithya Group (TSE:ALYA) reported lower second-quarter revenue and earnings from a year earlier, but cost reductions helped lift adjusted earnings and margins from the preceding quarter as bookings exceeded revenue.

Revenue fell 16.8% year over year to CAD 103.4 million. Adjusted EBITDA declined to CAD 8.3 million from CAD 12.8 million a year earlier, though it rose from CAD 5.4 million in the first quarter. The adjusted EBITDA margin was 8%, compared with 10.3% a year earlier and 5.2% in the first quarter.

President and CEO Paul Raymond said the company's strategic review remains active and is progressing as planned. The board is engaged with external advisers, he said, declining to comment on timing, parties or potential outcomes.

Cost cuts support sequential improvement

Selling, general and administrative expenses fell to CAD 25.2 million, down CAD 6.1 million, or 19.5%, from a year earlier. CFO Pierre Blanchette attributed the decrease primarily to lower employee compensation costs, including workforce reductions and variable compensation, as well as lower professional fees and share-based compensation. The decline also included the impact of the Datum divestiture.

Gross margin fell to CAD 32.5 million, or 31.4% of revenue, from CAD 42.8 million, or 34.4%, a year earlier. Blanchette cited lower revenue and utilization, changes in project mix, lower tax credits and a nonrecurring intellectual property sale in the prior-year period.

Alithya recorded a net loss of CAD 25 million, or CAD 0.26 per share, compared with a loss of CAD 31 million, or CAD 0.32 per share, a year earlier. The latest quarter included a CAD 30.4 million noncash goodwill impairment in the Industry Services and Solutions segment, related to restructuring in Quebec. Blanchette said the charge was unrelated to the strategic review.

Salesforce (CRM) stock closed on November 12, 2026, 13.1% below its October 22 high. Investors watching the slide want to know whether this is a chance to buy or a fall with further to go. No one can know that yet, but one thing is known for sure: how the stock behaved after its earlier sharp falls since 2010. So what happened to buyers who stepped in after those earlier drops?

Most Salesforce Dip Buyers Were Higher A Year Later

Since 2010, Salesforce stock has fallen more than 20% within 30 trading days on 12 separate occasions. In 8 of the 10 cases at least a year old, shares were higher 252 trading days later, posting a median gain of 32.5% over that year. The other two drops, in February and July 2026, are too recent to judge.

The two instances that lost money lost a lot. Shares bought on the January 5, 2022 dip traded 38% lower a year later. Those bought on the March 11, 2025 dip, the latest one old enough to judge, were down 29%.

Buyers usually sat through a further fall along the way. In the median case, the stock's lowest close in the following year sat 13.1% below its price on the dip date. Its best price in that year came after a median of 217 calendar days, about seven months.

Helmerich & Payne HP is set to release fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results on Nov. 18. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the to-be-reported quarter is a profit of 26 cents on revenues of $1.1 billion.

Let us delve into the factors that might have influenced the oil and gas drilling rig provider's performance in the September quarter. But it is worth taking a look at HP's previous quarter's performance first.

Highlights of Q3 Earnings & Surprise History

In the last reported quarter, this Tulsa, OK-based land and offshore contractor missed the consensus mark. Helmerich & Payne incurred an adjusted net loss per share of 11 cents in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, in sharp contrast with the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 11 cents in profit. Trend in Estimate Revision

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for the fiscal fourth-quarter bottom line has been unchanged in the past seven days. The estimated figure indicates a 2,700% year-over-year surge. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for revenues, meanwhile, suggests a 4,3% increase from the year-ago period.

Factors to Consider

Helmerich & Payne's fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 performance is likely to have benefited from stronger drilling activity in the United States. Lower 48, supported by healthy demand from private operators. The company reactivated 10 rigs in the third quarter, ending June with 147 operating rigs. Improved pricing and operational efficiencies, alongside higher rig utilization, could have lifted profitability. North America Solutions' direct margin guidance of $245-$255 million also suggests continued sequential improvement from the fiscal third quarter's $241 million.

Growing drilling activity in Argentina and recovering operations in the Middle East could have supported HP's fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 performance. The company planned to activate its 10th and 11th FlexRigs in Argentina by August 2026, backed by multi-year contracts. Meanwhile, five rig reactivations in Saudi Arabia brought its operating fleet to 22 rigs, while two suspended rigs in Bahrain resumed operations. Salesforce filed a shelf registration for 609,118 common shares tied to an ESOP offering, while expanding AI-led platforms like Agentforce and Data 360 and continuing large capital return programs.

The combination of AI product traction, government-focused Missionforce National Security wins, and targeted acquisitions in customer experience indicates that Salesforce is leaning into data-driven, automation-heavy use cases rather than relying only on traditional seat-based licensing.

The next area of focus will be how Salesforce's rapid Agentforce and Data 360 adoption reshapes the existing investment narrative around survival versus decline.

Scan beyond Salesforce and compare its AI driven pivot with a curated list of 41 profitable AI stocks that aren't just burning cash that already pair automation themes with real earnings power.

Salesforce Investment Narrative Recap

To own Salesforce, you need to believe the shift from seat-based licences to AI and data consumption can support the franchise that, according to michaelyang, a Simply Wall St Community investor who wrote the Narrative, is built around a governed customer record rather than just user counts. The near term catalyst sits in whether Agentforce and Data 360 adoption can offset any pressure on traditional subscription metrics.

The largest current risk is that debt funded capital returns and automation spending weigh on flexibility just as competition from platforms like Microsoft Copilot intensifies. The new ESOP related shelf registration looks operational rather than thesis changing, so the key watchpoint remains how AI product usage trends show up in upcoming earnings and cash flow.

The Cresta acquisition may be the cleanest link between the recent AI push and the short term setup. Voice agents plug directly into Salesforce's Agentforce and contact center stack, so execution here will help reveal whether management can translate AI interest into higher value workflow automation rather than just pilots.

If Cresta integrates well alongside Contentful and Data 360, that strengthens the argument michaelyang makes that the "meter" can shift from per seat to per action. If customers hesitate to route sensitive customer interactions and data through these new tools, that would raise questions around the durability of consumption based AI revenue as the main offset to any future licence pressure.

Based on those inputs, the narrative from michaelyang reaches a fair value of $255.90 for Salesforce by pairing 8.9% annual revenue growth with a future profit margin of 19.0%, then flowing those cash flows through a discounted cash flow framework that assumes the business simply endures.

title: Should You Buy HubSpot Stock For Its Cash?

Should You Buy HubSpot Stock For Its Cash?

HubSpot (HUBS) stock is worth a fresh look after falling 50.0% from its highest close of the past year of $405.83 on December 30, 2025. HubSpot's free cash flow over the last twelve months now equals 6.7% of its market value, against 4.2% for the median S&P 500 company. That yield marks either a business on sale or one the market expects to shrink. So is HubSpot a business on sale, or a shrinking one?

HubSpot's Free Cash Flow Has Grown For Three Years

So far, HubSpot's cash profile resembles that of a business on sale. Its twelve-month free cash flow climbed from $243 million in the period ended September 2023 to $677 million in the period ended September 2026, and it was higher at every quarter end in between.

This matters to an owner. Shareholders own a slice of the free cash a business produces, whether paid out or not, just as they own a slice of its profit. When the market recognizes cash retained inside a company, the share price tends to follow, especially when that cash is growing.

HubSpot sells its software by subscription, and that software costs little to deliver: the company kept 83.0% of its revenue as gross profit over the last twelve months, against 77.3% at Salesforce. Its capital spending took 25.3% of the cash its operations brought in. HubSpot turned 18.9% of its revenue into free cash flow, against 17.3% at Microsoft. Three other peers turned more: 34.5% at Salesforce, 20.1% at IBM and 40.8% at Adobe.

Reported profit is thinner: HubSpot's operating margin was 5.4% over the last twelve months, up from a loss of 1.6% of revenue a year earlier. HubSpot's stock-based compensation over the same twelve months was $504 million, about 14% of its $3.59 billion of revenue. And HubSpot does not need its cash to pay down borrowing: at the end of September 2026 it held $1.30 billion of cash and short-term investments, against $224 million of debt.

Why Is HubSpot's Growth Slowing?

HubSpot's growth is slowing because customers are taking longer to buy, management said on the November 4, 2026 call. Revenue growth from a year earlier fell in the second and third quarters of 2026, from 23.4% in fiscal Q1 2026 to 19.8% in fiscal Q2 and 17.1% in fiscal Q3. Management expects growth of 12% for fiscal Q4 2026.

Management says customers are buying differently in the AI era. They want to test AI on their own data before they pay, and HubSpot's move to free trials and pricing tied to outcomes has lengthened buying cycles. Larger customers bring more decision-makers into each deal, while smaller ones are more sensitive to price.

But while the market's attitude has gone sour, the reality remains that the underlying growth outlook is highly favorable for many companies directly benefiting from the revolution, with recent results from several underpinning the favorable picture.

Nebius Group NBIS, Snowflake SNOW, and Salesforce CRM have all recently posted strong results, with each currently sporting a favorable Zacks Rank, reflecting bullish earnings pictures.

Nebius Growth Remains Explosive

Nebius, a current Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), provides AI-focused cloud infrastructure, offering the computing capacity companies need to develop, train, and deploy advanced AI models. Shares have faced notable pressure recently, with concerns surrounding massive capital expenditures and financing needs weighing heavily.

EPS revisions have soared across the board over recent months.

Negative sentiment aside, the growth picture remains remarkably strong, with revenue in its latest release soaring 571% YoY to $981 million. Importantly, management expects 2027 sales in the $12-$13 billion range, roughly quadruple 2026 revenue.

The company's massive spending requirements do remain a concern, helping explain the weak post-earnings reaction and overall negative sentiment. But while the spending picture is undoubtedly aggressive, robust demand for AI infrastructure provides a favorable longer-term backdrop.

Snowflake Continues Benefiting From AI Adoption

Snowflake, a current Zacks Rank #2 (Buy), provides a cloud-based data platform that enables enterprises to store, analyze, and increasingly utilize their information for AI applications. EPS revisions for its current and next fiscal years have climbed consistently over the past year, suggesting growth rates of 78% in FY27 and 33% in FY28.

After years of unconditionally backing Jensen Huang and Nvidia (NASDAQ), Jim Cramer's confidence in the chipmaker has been shaken by the controversy surrounding its chief executive. And the reasons are understandable.

Cramer's investment thesis on Nvidia has always been closely tied to Huang's leadership. The CNBC host has repeatedly praised Huang as a visionary capable of transforming entire industries through artificial intelligence. He believed so strongly in Nvidia that he even named his dog after the company in 2017.

But with Huang's future now uncertain following allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy, Cramer's longtime conviction is facing a serious test. The controversy has raised questions about Huang's reputation and whether he can continue leading the company.

Cramer recently downgraded Nvidia from a buy to a hold, citing uncertainty surrounding the investigation.

Billionaires Ray Dalio and Philippe Laffont both trimmed their Nvidia stakes in the second quarter, even before this controversy began. See which AI stocks they still own.

That doesn't mean Cramer has turned bearish on the entire stock market (see what Cramer was buying last week).

While the Nvidia controversy and concerns about massive AI infrastructure spending have made him increasingly cautious, Cramer believes there are still plenty of attractive investment opportunities elsewhere.

During the recent CNBC Investing Club's annual meeting, Cramer and portfolio director Jeff Marks reviewed over 30 stocks in the Club's portfolio, identifying several companies they remain bullish on. Cramer has also continued to highlight investment opportunities outside the increasingly volatile AI trade.

Against this backdrop, we take a look at 10 stocks Jim Cramer is bullish on, ranked by the number of hedge funds holding stakes in them at the end of the second quarter of 2026.
